teach.title: No noun beside it
teach.say: Latin has no separate word for *he*, *she*, *it* or *they*. It uses a pointing word on its own, and then it is **a demonstrative used as a pronoun (is = he, ea = she, id = it)**, *prōnōmina dēmōnstrātīva substantīva*. Compare *is servus dormit* — that slave is asleep, a pointing word with its noun — and *is dormit* — he is asleep, the same word standing alone. Look beside it: if no noun matches it, read he, she or it.

teach.title: Its gender comes from the noun it stands for
teach.say: English picks *he*, *she* or *it* by whether the thing is male, female or neither. Latin picks by the gender of the noun being replaced, so a thing can be *is* or *ea*. *Ānulus* is masculine, so a ring is *is*; *gemma* is feminine, so a jewel is *ea*; *ōrnāmentum* is neuter, so it is *id*, and several of them are *ea*.

teach.title: When the pronoun is the object
teach.say: As the thing the verb acts on, the pronoun takes the accusative (the object form): **eum** (him), **eam** (her, it), **id** (it), and for more than one **eōs**, **eās**, **ea**. *Mārcus Quīntum videt et eum vocat* — sees Quintus and calls him. The gender still comes from the noun it replaces, not from the English.

teach.title: eius and eī: whose, and to whom
teach.say: **eius** means his, her or its — the genitive (the owner form), and it never changes for gender: *sacculus eius* = his purse. **eī** means to him, to her, to it — the dative (the receiver form): *Syra eī rosam dat* = Syra gives her a rose. Both stand outside the noun they belong to, so they are easy to miss.

teach.title: Pronoun, or pointing word?
teach.say: The same word does both jobs, and only the sentence around it decides. *Illa gemma magna est* — *illa* has *gemma* beside it, so it points: that jewel. *illam Lȳdia emit* — nothing matches *illam*, so it stands in for the jewel: Lydia buys it. Hunt for a noun agreeing in gender, number and case; if there is none, the word is a pronoun.

core.text: Latin has no separate words for *he, she, it, they*. It uses a pointing word without a noun: **a demonstrative used as a pronoun (is = he, ea = she, id = it)**, *prōnōmina dēmōnstrātīva substantīva*. *Is multōs servōs habet* = he has many slaves; *ea* = she; *id* = it; *iī / eae / ea* = they. The gender follows the noun replaced: cheese is *caseus*, so 'it' is *is*.
A pronoun stands in for a noun: *Marcus laughs; he is happy*. English picks *he / she / it* by real sex; Latin by the gender of the noun replaced.
A form of *is*, *hic* or *ille* with no noun beside it is a pronoun: he / she / it / they (or this one / that one), matching the noun it refers back to.

invented.en: Look at the cheese! It is bad.

core.text: The same word, two jobs. *Is servus dormit* — that slave sleeps (pointing word with a noun). *Is dormit* — he sleeps (pronoun, no noun). Look for a noun beside it matching in gender, number and case; if there is none, read he / she / it. Neuter *id* alone is 'it'.

more.text: From the learner's notes: a pronoun takes the place of a noun; any demonstrative can be used 'substantively' (standing alone), and *is, ea, id* is by far the commonest. *Hic* (this one) and *ille* (that one) do the same job with more point. Masculine for male persons and animals, feminine for female, neuter for everything else — but once a thing has a name, the pronoun takes the name's gender: *Ecce caseus! Is malus est*; *Aqua eius vītam nōn dat* (its water). *Huic malum dat, illī bonum* — he gives something bad to this one, something good to that one.

Ørberg cap. VIII: *eum / illum*, *eius*, *eī*, *eō*; *eam* from cap. III, *eōrum / eārum* from cap. V. The genitive *eius* means his / her / its when the owner is someone other than the subject (*sacculus eius*); for the subject's own, Latin uses *suus* (*sacculum suum pōnit*, r04:61.1). *Ille* can mean 'the famous', and *hic … ille* = the latter … the former. The true personal pronouns *ego*, *tū*, *nōs*, *vōs* have their own lesson. A&G §295–297.
